title: Pauri 4, meaning: the early hours
hookLine: what can we offer to see His court? In the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name; grace opens the door (Japji 4)

cards: What do you bring when you visit someone important? Flowers for a hostess. A bottle of something for the boss.
A card and a cake for a new neighbor. You stand at the door with something in your hands, hoping it's enough.
Guru Nanak's fourth pauri stands at a much bigger door, the court of the true Master, and asks exactly that question: what could anyone possibly bring?

teach.h: WHAT CAN WE BRING TO THE COURT?
teach.b: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. True is the Master, true His name, spoken with boundless love. People ask and beg, give, give, and the Giver gives.
Then the questions. What can we place before Him, so that His court comes into view? What words can we speak, so that hearing them He would love us?
The answer, the one camp three built a practice on: in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. Not flowers. Not a bottle.
Attention, in the quiet before dawn. Then a line people have argued over lovingly for centuries: karmee aavai kaparaa, nadree mokh duaar. Kaparaa is cloth, a garment.
Many read it as the body, the robe of this life, which comes by our karma, our actions.
Others read karam in its Persian sense, kindness or grace, so even the robe of honor comes by grace. Either way, the second half is the same: nadree mokh duaar. By His nadar, the door of liberation.
Nadar is a glance, a gaze, the look someone gives you when they're glad you came; it's the Persian nazar.
In Sikh teaching it's the gracious glance of the One, and the pauri says that's what finally opens the door. So the order is lovely. You show up early.
You bring attention, not payment. And the door is opened from the other side. The pauri ends: Nanak, know this; the One is all, and true.

how: Following Japji's fourth pauri, many Sikhs rise in the amrit vela before dawn for simran and Nitnem; nadar, the gracious glance, is spoken of throughout Sikh teaching as what finally opens the way.

o: a vow kept before the sun comes up
a gift you bring to the Guru's court
a gracious glance, a look of grace

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

s: the pauri says the court can be seen with a costly offering
the answer is the true Name, reflected on in the early hours.
nadar is related to the Persian word nazar, a glance
a gaze, the look of someone glad you came.
everyone reads karmee aavai kaparaa the same way
some read karma as actions, others karam as grace; the second half, by nadar the door, is the same.

games.q: you're standing at the door of the true Master's court, wondering what to bring. what does the pauri say?
o: a gift worth more than anyone else's.
the true Name, reflected on in the early hours.
games.why: in the amrit vela, reflect on the true Name and its greatness; by the gracious glance the door opens.

practice: The pauri points to the hours before dawn, and to bringing nothing: no requests, no list, no clever words, just your attention, set down like an empty cup.
If you pray, hold the true Name, Waheguru, and wait; if you don't, simply sit at the door and be awake.

wordCard.voice: Nadar. The gracious glance. In Japji's fourth pauri, by nadar comes the door of liberation.

orig.s: ਕਰਮੀ ਆਵੈ ਕਪੜਾ ਨਦਰੀ ਮੋਖੁ ਦੁਆਰੁ
orig.say: KAR-mee AA-vai KAP-raa, NAD-ree MOKH du-AAR
orig.note: Gurmukhi: by karam the garment, by nadar the door of liberation (Japji, pauri 4).

carryVoice: Your line: the early hour opens. You can't buy the glance, but you can be awake when it comes. That's day one hundred seventy.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 4
